name: bkde
title: Compute a Binned Kernel Density Estimate

origin.description: Returns x and y coordinates of the binned kernel density estimate of the probability density of the data.
origin.usage:
bkde(x, kernel = "normal", canonical = FALSE, bandwidth,
     gridsize = 401L, range.x, truncate = TRUE)

arguments.name: x
arguments.text: Numeric vector of observations from the distribution whose density is to be estimated. Missing values are not allowed.

arguments.name: bandwidth
arguments.text: Kernel bandwidth smoothing parameter. Larger values make smoother estimates. The default is a bandwidth computed from the variance of x, the oversmoothed bandwidth selector of Wand and Jones (1995, page 61).

arguments.name: kernel
arguments.text: Smoothing kernel: "normal" (Gaussian, the default), "box", "epanech" (centred beta(2,2)), "biweight" (centred beta(3,3)), or "triweight" (centred beta(4,4)).

arguments.name: canonical
arguments.text: If TRUE, canonically scaled kernels are used.

arguments.name: gridsize
arguments.text: Number of equally spaced points at which to estimate the density.

arguments.name: range.x
arguments.text: Minimum and maximum values of x at which to compute the estimate. The default is the minimum and maximum data values, extended by the support of the kernel.

arguments.name: truncate
arguments.text: If TRUE, data with x values outside range.x are ignored.

origin.details: This is the binned approximation to the ordinary kernel density estimate. Linear binning is used to obtain the bin counts. For each x value in the sample, the kernel is centered on that x and the heights of the kernel at each datapoint are summed. This sum, after a normalization, is the corresponding y value in the output.
origin.value: A list with x, the vector of sorted x values at which the estimate was computed, and y, the density estimates at those x values.

translation.description: Returns x and y coordinates of the binned kernel density estimate of the probability density of the data.
translation.usage:
bkde(x, kernel="normal", canonical=False, bandwidth=None,
     gridsize=401, range_x=None, truncate=True)

arguments.name: x
arguments.text: One-dimensional numeric sample from the distribution whose density is to be estimated. Missing values are not allowed.

arguments.name: bandwidth
arguments.text: Kernel bandwidth. Larger values make smoother estimates. None uses a bandwidth computed from the variance of x, the oversmoothed bandwidth selector of Wand and Jones (1995, page 61).

arguments.name: kernel
arguments.text: Smoothing kernel: "normal" (Gaussian, the default), "box", "epanech" (centred beta(2,2)), "biweight" (centred beta(3,3)), or "triweight" (centred beta(4,4)).

arguments.name: canonical
arguments.text: If True, canonically scaled kernels are used.

arguments.name: gridsize
arguments.text: Number of equally spaced points at which to estimate the density.

arguments.name: range_x
arguments.text: The two endpoints at which to compute the estimate. This is range.x in R. None uses the minimum and maximum data values, extended by the support of the kernel.

arguments.name: truncate
arguments.text: If True, observations outside range_x are ignored.

translation.details: This is the binned approximation to the ordinary kernel density estimate. Linear binning, from the Rust crate linbin, obtains the bin counts. Kernel weights and the FFT stay in NumPy. For each sample value, the kernel is centered there and the heights at the grid are combined. After normalization, that is the corresponding y value.
translation.value: A dict with x, the grid values at which the estimate was computed, and y, the density estimates at those x values.
translation.example:
from mass import geyser
from kernsmooth import bkde
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = geyser["duration"]
est = bkde(x, bandwidth=0.25)
plt.plot(est["x"], est["y"])
